thread.title: Here’s how you should prepare for a bear market in stocks

author: Howard Gold
title: Here’s how you should prepare for a bear market in stocks
text:
In my first column of 2019, I wrote “ we’re either entering or are in a bear market ,” and I don’t expect stocks to get back to their all-time highs. I could be wrong— there’s a reasonable chance stocks hit their lows on Christmas Eve —but with a slowing global economy, a tightening Federal Reserve and a bull market that already has stretched for almost a decade, risk is rising.
That’s why I think investors need to limit their downside rather than go for big gains. The easy money was made long ago in this market, and some of the recent highfliers—the FAANG stocks (Facebook FB, +2.91% Apple AAPL, +1.48% Amazon AMZN, +1.15% Netflix NFLX, -0.14% and Alphabet GOOG, -0.13% GOOGL, -0.06% parent of Google)— have been pummeled in recent weeks , raising big questions about where the leadership for a new, sustained leg of this bull market will come from.
As of Monday’s close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +0.55% had tacked on 1,700 points since the night before Christmas, while the S&P 500 SPX, +0.33% rose 8.4% and the Nasdaq Composite COMP, +0.39% gained 10%. But all three are still 13%-16% off their all-time highs set last year. ( Stocks rallied Tuesday morning too .)
This rally will likely continue, based on hope the Fed will hold off on rate increases this year, as desperate traders gleaned from some not-so-definitive remarks by Chairman Jerome Powell last week . Meanwhile, investors are betting trade talks between China and the U.S. will result in some kind of deal, which I think they will , and stocks have been trading higher in anticipation of the news.
To me, this looks like a classic relief rally, and as stocks move higher, risk-wary investors might consider taking profits. Those of you who are within five years of retirement should think about reducing your total equity holdings to 40% of your investible money. (For everyone else, 50%-60% in equities is fine, depending on your age.) That should give you enough downside protection to ignore further market selloffs and still have skin in the game to profit from sudden rallies.
My preferred ETFs for equities (I own them myself) are low-cost Vanguard Total Stock Market VTI, +0.40% and the Vanguard FTSE All World ex-US VEU, +0.35% I would consider putting three-quarters in the U.S. ETF and one-quarter in the other. If you want to be opportunistic with 5%-10% of your money, value stocks are a good bet. Since I wrote about them on Aug. 7, they’ve been outperforming the S&P—and certainly growth stocks, which have fallen badly out of favor. I think we’re at the start of a multiyear run for value , and I like Vanguard Value VTV, +0.15% and iShares Russell 1000 Value ETF IWD, +0.23% as good ways to play it.
In some ways, bonds are easier to invest in and in some ways they’re more difficult. Easier, because the stock selloff triggered a huge bond rally, driving the yield of the 10-year Treasury note TMUBMUSD10Y, +0.26% down to 2.55% (it’s now around 2.7%) from last year’s high of 3.23%. (Whatever happened to the bear market in bonds , by the way?) Right now bondholders have a chance to reduce both interest-rate sensitivity and credit risk.
Since I don’t see a recession in 2019 (but all bets are off for 2020), I think the Fed will continue to tighten, raising the federal-funds rate twice and continuing to reduce its balance sheet, which will help shorter-term yields rise. So I’ve shifted some money from long- and intermediate-term (3- to 7-year duration) bonds into shorter-term bonds (the two-year TMUBMUSD02Y, +1.13% currently yielding around 2.57%, looks like the sweet spot). This might be a good place to park some of the profits you take from equities.
Reducing credit risk will be particularly important if we do go into a recession. Half of all investment-grade bonds are one step away from junk status , so I would think about shifting money from investment-grade corporate bond funds into Treasury-only funds or (my preference) broader short-term bond index funds like the Vanguard Short-Term Bond BSV, -0.03% I’d also put 5% of my money into a gold ETF like SPDR Gold Trust GLD, -0.18% an inflation and crisis hedge. (Gold has been quietly doing very well lately.)
Things I’ve avoided forever: Emerging-market stocks and bonds , high-yield bonds and leveraged loans, popular yield vehicles for the last few years. There’s even less reason to jump into these now.
And one more thing: When risk rises, cash is king. Keeping 10% of your money in cash isn’t too much, or, if you’re close to retirement, consider selling enough of your equity investments to cover three years of expenses, after any expected income from a pension or Social Security. That will help you ride out any coming bear market and provide some cash to put into stocks again when the storm passes and the sky clears.
Howard R. Gold is a MarketWatch columnist. Follow him on Twitter @howardrgold . He owns many of the ETFs he cited in this column.
